chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
"If a male slave has a female slave under his ownership and he divorces her, and then his master frees her, she remains with him in a single state of marriage."

So he said: How can you say that his divorce does not take effect, while this report establishes that his divorce is effective? For if it were not effective, the female slave would have two divorces with him.

It was said to him: The meaning in this report and what follows its pattern, which includes this meaning, is that if a slave is married to a female slave who is not his master's, his divorce is valid.
And we prevented his divorce only when both (the slave and the female slave) belong to one man, and we have already explained that previously.
And what clarifies it further is what has been narrated:

key_terms.أَمَةِ غَيْرِ مَوْلَاهُ: A female slave not belonging to his master
key_terms.وَاحِدَةٍ: One state (referring to a single marriage bond)

ai.seo_question: Does a slave's divorce take effect if he divorces a female slave who belongs to a different master?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi uses this narration from Imam al-Sadiq to resolve the juristic debate regarding the validity of a slave's divorce when his wife belongs to a different master. The text clarifies that while dual masters restrict the slave's unilateral authority, separate ownership allows the divorce to take effect, illustrating the nuanced application of property rights in Shia family law. This distinction highlights how ownership structure directly influences the legal capacity of slaves in marital contracts.
